summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct between men and women has not been criminalised in Suriname since 1869, and the country overview maintained by Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, records it as legal nationwide. A revision carried out after the 2011 Universal Periodic Review equalised the age of consent for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

In March 2015 the Penal Code was amended so that Articles 175, 175a and 176 reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation. Protection outside those provisions rests on an implied reading rather than an explicit statute: Article 8.2 of the Surinamese Constitution lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds, and the LGBT Platform Suriname has repeatedly called for a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Legal gender recognition is not available. The State has not brought its law on recognition of gender identity into line with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights judgment on the subject; at the July 2024 review of Suriname by the UN Human Rights Committee, experts pressed the delegation on implementing that judgment, and the meeting summary records no implementation.

Discrimination and violence persist in practice. The US State Department's 2015 human rights report for Suriname documented discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities. A joint submission to the Human Rights Committee by LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata states that despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation.

Organisational space exists on paper: LGBTI organisations can register. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded on 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, the New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action. The platform reports that it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 Penal Code revision that added sexual-orientation discrimination provisions also abolished the death penalty; the Military Code followed in 2021. Both were welcomed by the Human Rights Committee at its July 2024 review.

The State told the Human Rights Committee that its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, and pointed to monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission as evidence of that commitment. The Committee's experts nonetheless returned to the gap between the constitutional guarantee and the recognition of transgender identity.

The US State Department's reporting on Suriname from 2015 also covers police brutality and corruption and the Bouterse trial. These are not trans-specific findings, but they describe the enforcement environment in which the discrimination and violence documented for LGBTI persons occurs.
localsOnly:
The LGBT Platform Suriname was founded on 29 August 2011 and brings together five member organisations: PAREA, the New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action. LGBTI organisations are able to register in the country.

The platform has repeatedly asked to take part in state consultative processes and reports being left out of them. Its stated legislative demand is a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability, which would replace reliance on the constitutional 'any other status' clause.

The State cites the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission among the monitoring bodies that back its anti-discrimination commitments.
outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved on this evidence whether the March 2015 Penal Code amendments reach gender identity as a ground distinct from sexual orientation; the sources reviewed frame them in terms of sexual orientation.

Whether the Inter-American Court of Human Rights judgment on recognition of gender identity has been implemented in Surinamese law is not settled by the sources: the July 2024 Human Rights Committee session shows experts raising it and no implementation recorded in the meeting summary. The practical route, if any, for changing legal gender markers is not sourced here.

The most recent first-hand documentation of discrimination and violence in the sources reviewed dates from 2015 to 2024. Conditions after that period are not sourced, and the absence of a recorded incident should not be read as an absence of risk.

No source reviewed records prosecutions or penalties under Penal Code Articles 175, 175a or 176 as applied to anti-LGBTI hate speech or discrimination, so enforcement of the 2015 amendments is unverified.
